overview:
Mongolia is a vast, high, dry country squeezed between Russia and China, about the size of Alaska, with fewer people for its size than almost anywhere on Earth. Only around 3.5 million people live in a land of some 1.56 million km², and roughly half of them are in the capital, Ulan Bator, also written Ulaanbaatar, which is the coldest capital city in the world.

Mongolian is the national language, written both in the Cyrillic alphabet and in a traditional upright script that runs from top to bottom. Mongolia is a republic with an elected president and parliament. Perhaps a quarter of the population still lives as herders, moving with sheep, goats, horses, cattle and camels between seasonal pastures and living in gers, round felt tents that can be taken down and packed onto a truck in about an hour. Mining copper, coal and gold is the biggest industry, and cashmere from Mongolian goats is exported worldwide.
landAndNature: Mongolia is high and dry, averaging about 1,580 meters above sea level and far from any ocean. The Gobi spreads across the south, a stony rather than sandy desert where dinosaur fossils lie so near the surface that whole nests of eggs have been uncovered. Grassy steppe covers the center, forest and taiga rise in the north near Siberia, and the Altai peaks in the west carry glaciers. Winters drop below minus 30 degrees Celsius, and a harsh winter called a dzud can kill millions of animals. Snow leopards, gray wolves, wild Bactrian camels and Przewalski's horse, the last truly wild horse, live here.
peopleAndCulture: Herding shapes daily life: families eat mutton, steamed dumplings called buuz, and dairy foods including dried curd and airag, fermented mare's milk. A guest in a ger is always offered food and a place to sit. The three games of the Naadam festival each July are wrestling, archery and horse racing, in which children ride for more than 20 kilometers across open country. Throat singers produce two notes at once, a deep drone with a whistling melody above it, and the morin khuur, a horsehead fiddle, is the national instrument. Some western Mongolian hunters still ride out with trained golden eagles.
history: Nomadic empires rose and fell on these grasslands for thousands of years. In 1206 Temujin united the tribes and took the title Genghis Khan, building the largest connected land empire in history, which under his grandson Kublai Khan reached from Korea to Hungary and ruled China. The empire eventually broke apart, and from the 1600s Mongolia came under Chinese Qing rule. Mongolia declared independence in 1911 and, with Soviet backing, became a communist state in 1924, closely tied to the Soviet Union for nearly seventy years; monasteries were destroyed and monks killed in the 1930s. Peaceful protests in 1990 brought democracy, and Mongolia has held free elections since.
funFacts: Mongolia has one of the lowest population densities on Earth, with roughly two people per square kilometer.
Ulan Bator is the coldest national capital in the world, with winter temperatures falling below minus 30 degrees Celsius.
The Gobi Desert has produced some of the richest dinosaur finds anywhere, including nests of fossilized eggs.
Genghis Khan's empire became the largest connected land empire in history, stretching from Korea to eastern Europe.
At the Naadam horse races the jockeys are children, and the horses gallop over 20 kilometers of open steppe.
